latest_final: A man killed his wife. He did it himself, deliberately and with intent, with no accident, no consent and no self-defence, and he knows the responsibility is his. She is dead and can never come back. What he is doing now is preparing the deception that will cover it: he is practising her handwriting, writing the same line over and over until he can imitate her hand, seven attempts of "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back"—set in her voice and addressed to him. Once the imitation is convincing, a letter written that way is to be "found" as something she left behind. Whoever finds it is meant to believe she was disappointed in him and walked out for good, never returning; that explains why she is no longer there, keeps anyone from learning that she died, and stops them looking for her. The author is not after money or advantage, nobody has yet been taken in, and the forgery has not been spotted. Looking at the seven practised copies, he sighs, "I know I'm in trouble": the fake is what stands between him and being found out, and if the imitation is ever seen through, both the death and his responsibility for it will be exposed.
